Empirical Research Plan  
“Credibly Estimating the Effects of Schooling, Union Membership, Immigration, Military Service, and Class Size on Labor-Market and Educational Outcomes”

To keep the exposition organized, I lay out five parallel research designs—one for each policy question—because the institutional setting naturally calls for a different quasi-experimental strategy in each case.  Section 5 provides fully-worked R code for Design 1 (returns to schooling), the template most readers will find easiest to replicate.  The same coding skeleton can be adapted to the other designs by swapping in the relevant data and variables.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Design 1 – Schooling: Two–Stage Least Squares (Instrumental Variables)  
 Instrument = Quarter-of-Birth (QOB) dummies that exploit compulsory-schooling drop-out rules.

Design 2 – Union Membership: Regression Discontinuity in NLRB Certification Elections  
 Running variable = “yes” vote share in the certification election; cutoff = 50 percent.

Design 3 – Immigration (Mariel Boatlift): Difference-in-Differences / Event Study  
 Treatment = Miami after 1980; Controls = Weighted average of four comparison cities.

Design 4 – Military Service (Vietnam draft): Instrumental Variables  
 Instrument = Draft-lottery number (≤ 122 treated in 1970; ≤ 95 in 1971; etc.).

Design 5 – Class Size (Israel, Maimonides’ Rule): Sharp Regression Discontinuity  
 Running variable = Enrollment in grade g, school s; cutoff = multiples of 40.

Pairing each outcome with the quasi-experiment that most closely meets the requisite identification assumptions maximizes credibility.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Design 1 – Returns to Schooling  
• Treatment variable: Completed years of schooling (continuous).  
• Instrument / “encouragement”: Born in Q1, Q2, Q3 vs Q4 of the calendar year.  
• Sample: U.S.‐born white male cohorts 1930–1959, observed in 1980–2000 Censuses or ACS.  
• Outcome: log(weekly earnings).  

Design 2 – Union Effect on Wages  
• Treatment: Worker covered by a collective-bargaining agreement one year after a close election.  
• Control: Observations where the union lost the election by < 2 p.p.  
• Cutoff date: Election date (event time t=0).  

Design 3 – Mariel Boatlift  
• Treatment group: Residents of Miami in survey years 1981–1990.  
• Controls: Residents of Atlanta, Houston, Los Angeles, and Tampa/St. Petersburg.  
• Pre-period: 1974–1979 CPS ORG.  

Design 4 – Veteran Status  
• Treatment: Draft-eligible men (lottery number ≤ cutoff) in birth cohorts 1944–1952.  
• Control: Men with lottery numbers above the cutoff.  
• Outcome: Log annual earnings from Social-Security records 1974–1990.  

Design 5 – Class Size  
• Treatment: Pupils in classes that were split because enrollment exceeded 40, 80, 120…  
• Control: Pupils in classes just below each multiple of 40.  
• Outcome: Fifth-grade test score (z-score).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Across designs we rely on four generic assumptions; here they are specialized to each:

A1. Relevance  
– QOB must predict schooling (Design 1). Empirically strong F > 25 in U.S. data.  
– Vote share must sharply determine certification (Design 2, graph the first-stage).  
– Boatlift must increase Miami’s labor supply but not comparison cities (Design 3).  
– Low lottery numbers must raise likelihood of service (Design 4).  
– Enrollment must jump class size exactly at multiples of 40 (Design 5).  

A2. As-good-as-random (Independence / Local Randomization)  
– Quarter-of-birth is orthogonal to ability and parental SES once we control for State×Year (Design 1).  
– Close elections are quasi-random (Design 2).  
– Absent the Boatlift, Miami wage trend would have paralleled controls (Design 3).  
– Lottery numbers are literally random (Design 4).  
– Schools cannot precisely manipulate enrollment to avoid the split (Design 5: McCrary test).  

A3. Exclusion / Stable Unit Treatment Value  
– QOB affects adult earnings only through schooling, not via birth-season health shocks (plausible for mature cohorts).  
– In Design 2 spillovers are minimal because RDD is local.  
– Design 3 requires no economy-wide shocks hitting Miami alone in 1980.  
– Draft eligibility influences income only through veteran status.  
– In Design 5 splitting does not change curriculum except via class size.  

A4. Monotonicity (IV designs) / Parallel Trends (DID) / Continuity (RDD) hold as appropriate.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification and Remedies
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1 (Design 1): Season-of-birth correlated with parental background or health.  
 Remedy: Control for race, sex, cohort, and include State-of-birth×Year-of-birth fixed effects; check covariate balance.

T2 (Design 3): Miami might have had differential demand shocks (e.g., tourism boom).  
 Remedy: Event-study plot; placebo DID on pre-Boatlift years; add city-specific linear trends.

T3 (Design 5): Manipulation of running variable (schools could hold students back).  
 Remedy: McCrary density test; exclude grades where bunching is evident; local-linear RDD with bias-corrected inference.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline (Design 1 example: Returns to Schooling) 
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 0.  Libraries
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # Fast data wrangling
library(fixest)       # IV and high-dim FE regressions
library(estimatr)     # Robust SEs
library(ggplot2)      # Plots

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 1.  Data Loading
# Assume 'census80.csv' contains individual microdata with the
# variables: yob, mob, stateb, educ, lweekly_earn, race, sex.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
c80  <- fread("census80.csv")         # 1% 1980 IPUMS sample
c90  <- fread("census90.csv")         # 1990 5% sample
data <- rbindlist(list(c80, c90), use.names = TRUE, fill = TRUE)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.  Variable Construction
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
data[, qob := fifelse(mob %in% 1:3, 1,
               fifelse(mob %in% 4:6, 2,
               fifelse(mob %in% 7:9, 3, 4)))]

# Instrument set: use three dummies Q1, Q2, Q3; Q4 is reference
data[, `:=`(Q1 = as.integer(qob == 1),
            Q2 = as.integer(qob == 2),
            Q3 = as.integer(qob == 3))]

# Outcome and treatment
data[, ln_earn := log(lweekly_earn)]

# Keep prime-age men to minimize labor-supply selection
sample <- data[race == "White" & sex == "Male" & age %between% c(25, 59)]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3.  Main 2SLS Specification
# ln(wage) = β * schooling + Xγ + ε
# schooling instrumented with Q1-Q3 dummies
# FE: StateBirth × YOB (year-of-birth)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
iv_spec <- feols(ln_earn ~ 1 | 
                   educ ~ Q1 + Q2 + Q3 | 
                   stateb^yob, 
                 data = sample, 
                 cluster = ~stateb*yob)

summary(iv_spec)
etable(iv_spec, se = "cluster")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.  First-Stage F-Statistic
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
iv_first <- iv_spec$iv_first_stage
print(iv_first$diagnostics)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 5.  Robustness Check: Add Quadratic in YOB and Census Year FE
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
sample[, yob_sq := (yob - mean(yob))^2]

iv_rob <- feols(ln_earn ~ yob + yob_sq | 
                  educ ~ Q1 + Q2 + Q3 | 
                  stateb + yob, 
                data = sample, 
                cluster = ~stateb*yob)

etable(list(Main = iv_spec, "+YOB trend" = iv_rob), se = "cluster")
```

To replicate other designs:  
• Swap in election-level data and replace the `feols()` call with `rdrobust()` for Design 2.  
• Use `did2s` or `fixest` two-way FE for the Mariel DID.  
• Add the draft-lottery variable as an instrument (`ivreg` or `feols`) for Design 4.  
• Run bias-corrected local-linear RDD with `rdrobust` for Design 5.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Design 1 – Each additional year of schooling should raise log weekly earnings by ≈ 7-9 percent (β ≈ 0.07–0.09).  

Design 2 – Union coverage is expected to lift wages by ~10–15 percent for workers around the cutoff.  

Design 3 – Canonical estimates find essentially zero effect of the Mariel Boatlift on native wages or employment (β ≈ 0).  

Design 4 – Vietnam service likely lowers civilian earnings by 10–12 percent in the 1970s, fading to ≈ 0 by the late 1980s.  

Design 5 – A one-student reduction in class size (~25 → 24) should increase test scores by ≈ 0.02–0.04 σ.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Design 1: IV)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Instrument relevance (F > 25) ………………… 1  
C2: Independence / random assignment of QOB …. 0.8 (seasonality concerns)  
C3: Exclusion restriction ……………………………… 0.8  
C4: Monotonicity (no “defiers”) …………………… 1  
C5: No heterogeneous treatment effect biases … 0.7  

Aggregate score ≈ 4.3 / 5 → Reasonably credible, but sensitivity analyses are essential.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
This multi-design blueprint demonstrates how researchers can tailor a causal inference strategy to each institutional setting while relying on the same underlying empirical toolkit.
